title: How much is jaggery equal to a child's weight worth?
description: Jaggery equal to the weight of one child and wheat equal to the weight of another are to be donated. We assume sensible weights and prices for one kilogram, then multiply to estimate the worth of each. Keeko doubts that the worth is the weight plus the cost.
teaching_notes: One idea: the worth of goods is the weight in kilograms times the cost of one kilogram. Watch for students who add the weight and the cost instead of multiplying.

source: Estimate the worth of jaggery equal to Roxie's weight and wheat equal to Estu's weight
video_script.why: To estimate a worth we describe how the quantities relate, assume sensible values for the unknowns, and then multiply the weight by the cost of one kilogram.
video_script.substitution: Write worth as weight in kilograms times the cost of one kilogram, put in sensible assumed values, and multiply.
video_script.anchor: jaggery and wheat equal to the weight of a child
video_script.wrong_answer: the worth is the weight plus the cost
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko adds 45 and 70 to get 115. But 70 rupees pays for only one kilogram, so 45 kilograms cost 70 rupees forty five times; we multiply.
video_script.payoff_line: The worth is the weight times the cost of one kilogram

final_answer.value: About 3150 rupees of jaggery and about 2500 rupees of wheat
final_answer.spoken: The jaggery is worth about three thousand one hundred fifty rupees. The wheat is worth about two thousand five hundred rupees.

names.Laksh: the eleven year old whose weight sets the wheat
names.Ruhee: the thirteen year old whose weight sets the jaggery
names.Jia: the person who plans to donate jaggery and wheat

maths_rules: worth of jaggery = weight in kg × cost of 1 kg of jaggery
assume 45 kg and 70 rupees for 1 kg: 45 × 70 = 3150
worth of wheat = weight in kg × cost of 1 kg of wheat
assume 50 kg and 50 rupees for 1 kg: 50 × 50 = 2500
the slip: 45 + 70 = 115 adds a weight to a price, which makes no sense
video_script.design: The two donations sit side by side. Each has a small line showing weight and the cost of one kilogram, then the multiplication is built beneath it.
open_questions: The weights 45 kg and 50 kg and the prices 70 and 50 rupees are the book's own assumptions.

<bookmark mark='five'/>Five times five is twenty five.
<bookmark mark='zero'/>Each fifty has one zero, so two zeroes follow.
